item.title: How Much Does EV Charging Add to Your Electric Bill?
item.description:
Quick Answer

Expect an extra $30–$60 per month for a typical US driver. That's roughly 320 kWh of home charging (about 13,500 miles a year at 3–4 miles per kWh) at typical residential rates. Off-peak time-of-use charging can cut that meaningfully — while DC fast charging runs 2–4× home rates and should stay a road-trip tool, not a habit.

The bill comes down to three numbers.

  • Miles driven — the average US driver covers about 1,100 miles a month.
  • Efficiency — typical EVs run 3–4 miles per kWh; big trucks can be near 2.
  • Your rate and timing — flat vs time-of-use decides the multiplier.

Run the full math in the three numbers, or compare directly with gasoline costs. New to the units? Start with what a kWh actually is.

item.title: Time-of-Use Electricity Rates: When Power Is Cheapest and How to Save
item.description:
Quick Answer

Time-of-Use (TOU) rates charge different prices by time of day — typically $0.12–$0.15/kWh off-peak vs. $0.25–$0.40/kWh on-peak (usually 4–9 PM weekdays). Shifting laundry, EV charging, dishwashing, and pool pumps to overnight or weekend off-peak windows can cut your electric bill 15–25%.

  • Off-peak hours (nights, early mornings, weekends) carry the lowest rates
  • On-peak hours (typically 4–9 PM weekdays) cost 2–3× more
  • Shift 50% of usage to off-peak to save roughly $30–$60/month

If your utility has offered you a time-of-use rate plan, whether it saves money depends on when you use power. Households that can move most of their usage to off-peak windows save 15–25% on the same kWh; households that can’t shift much often pay more. Your peak-to-off-peak price ratio, how much load you can move, and your current usage pattern are the three numbers that decide it.
